newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline prices fall sharply as stocks pile up.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline prices fall sharply as stocks pile up.

text.p: Gasoline prices fell in New York Wednesday after a weekly report showed a much larger-than-expected buildup in gasoline stocks.

"Gasoline had been strong versus the rest of the market, but after this strong build due to high production, there was a lot of profit-taking," said Dale Wong, senior trader at Nationsbanc-CRT in Houston.
Gasoline for December delivery ended off 0.98 cents at 63.63 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) said on Tuesday evening that gasoline stocks grew 4.7 million barrels for the week ended November 1 after the API reported a drop of 3.8 million barrels the week before.
The market had anticipated gasoline inventory levels to remain about the same.

An unexpected drop in total distillate stocks, which includes heating oil, sent heating oil prices higher. December heating oil rose 1.03 cents to 66.45 cents a gallon. The API said total distillate stocks dropped 429,000 barrels.
Colder temperatures expected in the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world, also supported prices, dealers said.
December crude oil rose 5 cents to $22.69 a barrel at NYMEX. Crude had risen as high as $23.15 a barrel on the strength of heating oil before succumbing to weakness.
"We followed gasoline lower towards the end of the day. Some guys smelled blood," one trader said.
Precious metals also fell, led by silver, as investors ploughed money into stocks after President Clinton won re-election and Republicans retained control of Congress.
"The whole complex continues to erode with silver rotting on the vine," FIMAT trader John Tyree said.
Dealers also said the continued strength of the dollar was hurting demand in Asia.
December silver on New York's Commodity Exchange (COMEX) fell 8 cents to $4.713 an ounce while December gold closed down 90 cents at $378.70 an ounce.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures rose 0.90 points to 237.03, boosted partly by strength in the Chicago Board of Trade's soybean complex.
Soybean futures closed sharply higher boosted partly by a bullish crop forecast by Memphis-based analytical firm Sparks Companies.
"We followed Sparks. He set the tone and that's the tune we danced to," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
Sparks put U.S. production this year at 2.367 billion bushels, only marginally above the U.S. Department of Agriculture's projection last month of 2.346 billion.
Traders said the market was braced for a soybean production tally of nearer 2.4 billion bushels and USDA is expected to upwardly revise its estimate next week.
November soybeans rose 11 cents to $6.81 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
